This Is a Wiring Difference. Not a Behavior Problem.
The Repetitive Play Loop
When a child spins a wheel, their visual cortex receives powerful, predictable, self-generated sensory feedback. This activates the dopaminergic reward pathway — the same pathway involved in all pleasurable experiences.
In many children with ASD, this loop runs more powerfully than typical, and the prefrontal cortex's ability to redirect toward novel, open-ended play is reduced. The basal ganglia — the brain's habit-formation center — locks in these patterns because they feel deeply satisfying at a neurological level.
This is not stubbornness. This is not a parenting failure. This is a brain that has found a highly reliable source of sensory regulation — and keeps returning to it.
What This Means for You
Not Broken
Your child is not broken — their brain is wired differently, seeking reliable input.
Not Intentional
They are not doing this to frustrate you. The pattern serves a neurological function.
Channelable
This function can be channeled and expanded — not simply blocked or suppressed.
Modifiable
With the right materials, functional play can become equally or more satisfying.
Your Child Is Here. Here Is Where We're Heading.
Unusual toy use typically means a child has mastered the exploratory/sensorimotor stage so well that they keep returning to it — because it's reliable, satisfying, and demands nothing socially. The goal is NOT to eliminate what works. It is to expand their repertoire.
0–12 Months: Exploratory
Mouthing, shaking, banging, dropping objects to explore
12–18 Months: Relational
Putting in/out, stacking, combining objects — beginning relationships
18–24 Months: Functional
Using toys for intended purpose: driving cars, building with blocks
24–36 Months: Early Symbolic
Pretending with props: feeding a doll, putting a toy to sleep
3–5 Years: Complex Pretend
Cooperative play, roles, narratives, peer scenarios

High-Plasticity Window (18 months – 6 years): With targeted intervention during this period, play skill development can expand significantly. Every week of intervention in this window is high-yield.

The Technique: Material-Based Play Expansion
Parent-Friendly Alias: "The 9 Toys That Teach Playing"
Material-Based Play Expansion is the clinical practice of selecting and introducing specific therapeutic toys and materials that bridge a child's existing sensory-driven play patterns toward functional play (using toys for their intended purpose) and eventually symbolic play (pretending). Rather than eliminating what the child loves about repetitive play, this approach uses strategically chosen materials to make intended toy use equally or more rewarding than the repetitive pattern — thereby expanding the play repertoire through the child's own motivation.
Domain
DEV-PLY | Pediatric Play Development
Ages
18 months – 8 years
Duration
10–20 min/session
Frequency
Daily | Setting: Home
This Technique Crosses Therapy Boundaries
Because the brain doesn't organize by therapy type, five distinct disciplines each play a critical role in material-based play expansion. Together they form the Pinnacle FusionModule™ — one child, one plan, five perspectives.
Occupational Therapist (Primary Lead)
Selects materials based on the child's sensory profile — matching toys to the sensory input the child seeks, then expanding from there. Assesses play development stage and designs the progression pathway.
Speech-Language Pathologist
Uses these same materials to target joint attention, requesting communication, labeling, and turn-taking — embedding language targets within the play interaction that materials naturally create.
ABA / BCBA Therapist
Designs the reinforcement schedule around material use — using the child's attraction to the toy as the natural reinforcer, and shaping functional play through differential reinforcement.
Special Educator
Uses materials in structured play sessions at school, teaching play scripts and generalizing skills across settings — ensuring what's learned at home transfers to the classroom.
NeuroDevelopmental Pediatrician
Oversees the diagnostic framework, identifies co-occurring conditions, and monitors developmental progression against standardized milestones.
This Is Not a Random Activity. It Is a Precision Tool.
Every session is designed to hit specific, measurable developmental targets — from the immediate functional play goal all the way through to school readiness and social communication.

Material 1: Cause-Effect Toys
Canon Category: Cause-Effect / Switch Toys
₹400–1,500
Push this → that happens. Predictable reward for intentional action. Cause-effect toys create a powerful, satisfying loop: the child acts intentionally and the toy responds reliably. This is the neurological bridge between sensory-seeking and purposeful play.
Why It Works
Same neurological principle as spinning — intentional action produces predictable, satisfying outcome. But now the child is using the toy as designed.
Best options: Pop-up pals, ball drop towers, musical busy boxes
Pinnacle Recommends
Dyomnizy Educational Memory Game with Lights & Sound
🛒 Amazon.in — ₹519 ✅ Active Stock
The therapeutic action: Place toy in front of child. Model pressing the button/switch. Wait for child's response. If child presses: celebrate immediately. If child tries to spin toy: gently reorient to the button — "Here's the button — watch what happens!" Duration: 3–5 minutes.
Material 2: Vehicles with Ramps & Tracks
Canon Category: Problem-Solving Toys
₹300–1,200
Makes driving more rewarding than wheel-spinning. Structure channels interest. When a car zooms down a ramp, it delivers powerful sensory feedback — speed, sound, impact — that competes directly with the satisfaction of spinning wheels. The ramp becomes the new ritual.
Why It Works
The zoom provides sensory feedback that competes with wheel-spinning on equal neurological footing. The structural constraint makes "driving" the exciting choice.
Best options: Car ramps, wooden train tracks, marble runs
The Therapeutic Action
Set up ramp. Place car at top. Build anticipation: "Ready? Ready? Ready? GO!" Release. Let the excitement of the zoom be organic. If child grabs car to flip and spin: "Let's put it back on the ramp — watch it zoom!" Redirect without conflict. Duration: 3–5 minutes of ramp use.
🛒 Search Amazon.in: "car ramp toy India"
Material 3: Simple Pretend Play Sets
Canon Category: Sorting / Categorization
₹300–1,000
Clear functions teach what toys are for. A pot is for stirring. A brush is for hair. A phone is for talking. Simple pretend sets with obvious, single-function objects are the most direct path from exploratory play to functional play.
Why It Works
Realistic objects with unmistakable purpose anchor the concept that this thing does this specific thing — the cognitive foundation of all functional play.
Best options: Simple kitchen (3–5 pieces), baby care set, tool bench
The Therapeutic Action
Model ONE simple function (stir the pot). No complex narrative. "Stir, stir, stir!" After 3 models, offer spoon to child. If child stirs even once — major celebration. Don't layer in feeding or complex scenarios until stirring is mastered. Duration: 5 minutes of single function.
🛒 Search Amazon.in: "pretend play set India"
Material 4: Sensory-Match Toys
Canon Category: Problem-Solving Toys
₹350–1,200
Meet them where they are. If they love spinning → gear toys. If they love lining → train tracks. If they love flipping → lift-the-flap books. Sensory-match toys are designed to deliver the same sensory satisfaction the child already seeks — but as the toy's intended function.
Why It Works
The function-matching IS the therapy. No redirection needed when the toy was designed for the sensory input the child craves.
Best options: Interlocking gear toys, domino runs, spin art, lift-the-flap books
The Therapeutic Action
FOR SPINNERS: Place gear toy, spin one gear, watch child's face.
FOR LINERS: Begin building train track, place one piece, leave space for child to add next.
The sensory preference is the entry point — the toy expands it into functional use. Duration: 5 minutes.
🛒 Search Amazon.in: "gear toy for kids India"
Material 5: Action Figures with Movement
Canon Category: Problem-Solving Toys
₹300–1,000
Characters that do things invite real play. Static figures just get lined up. But a bendable figure that walks, sits, and holds things? That figure becomes an agent — and agency is the seed of symbolic play.
Why It Works
Character-as-agent is the core therapeutic concept. When a figure can act, the child learns that objects represent beings — the cognitive leap that unlocks pretend play.
Best options: Bendable figures from preferred shows, vehicles with figure sizing
The Therapeutic Action
Make the figure DO something simple — walk it across the floor toward child. Narrate minimally: "He's walking. He's going to the car." Child's spontaneous interaction with the figure counts as functional play.
The physical form is secondary — the concept of character-as-agent is what matters. Duration: 3–5 minutes.
🛒 Search Amazon.in: "action figure moveable India"
Material 6: Bubbles & Wands
Canon Category: Transition Objects / Comfort Items
₹50–300
Cannot be lined up. Cannot be spun. Cannot be flipped. Bubbles are the great equalizer — they demand functional interaction simply by existing. Chasing a bubble, popping a bubble, blowing a bubble: every interaction is play as it was meant to be.
Why It Works
Pure functional play that creates shared joy. The natural pause after bubbles disappear teaches requesting — the child must communicate for more.
Best options: Large wand set, bubble gun, touchable no-spill bubbles
The Therapeutic Action
Blow or wave bubbles without directing child. Let the bubbles do the work. When child reacts — pause, wait for communicative attempt (any gesture, vocalization, eye contact) before making more. This natural pause teaches requesting.
Duration: 5 minutes. Universal starting point — works across all sensory profiles.
🛒 Search Amazon.in: "bubble wand set India"
Material 7: Construction with Purpose
Canon Category: Problem-Solving / Sorting
₹400–1,500
Building that creates something functional gives construction meaning beyond the act. The key word is "purpose." Building a tower to knock it down is still exploratory play. Building a car you then drive — that is the threshold of functional play.
Why It Works
Structure + purposeful outcome = the neurological target. The post-build play is as important as the construction itself.
Best options: Magnetic tiles (Magna-Tiles style), Duplo vehicle kits
The Therapeutic Action
Start a build WITH a clear goal: "We're making a car!" Narrate the steps. Let child add pieces. When construction is complete: play with it. Drive the car. Knock the structure. The post-build play is the therapeutic target.
Duration: 10 minutes total — 5 for building, 5 for play.
🛒 Search Amazon.in: "magnetic tiles building set India"
Material 8: Puppets & Character Toys
Canon Category: Transition Objects / Comfort Items
₹200–800
Characters that model pretend play and reduce the demand of direct social interaction. A puppet is a safe intermediary — the child can respond to the puppet without the full social weight of responding to an adult. This makes puppets a powerful bridge to symbolic play.
Why It Works
The character function is what matters, not commercial production quality. Puppets create a socially low-demand context for practicing pretend interaction.
Best options: Hand puppets (animal), finger puppet sets, character puppets
The Therapeutic Action
Bring puppet "alive" with simple personality. Puppet greets child. Puppet does something simple (eats pretend food). If child ignores puppet: puppet approaches quietly, makes minimal sound, retreats. Never force puppet interaction.
Duration: 5 minutes. Let curiosity be the entry point.
🛒 Search Amazon.in: "hand puppet toy India"
Material 9: Sensory Bins with Tasks
Canon Category: Sorting / Categorization
₹250–800
Preferred sensory input becomes the vehicle for purposeful play. The bin gives the child what they already crave — rich, immersive sensory experience. But embedded tasks turn that experience into purposeful, directed play.
Why It Works
Same sensory engagement the child seeks — but now with task structure embedded within it. The sensory reward is the entry; the task is the growth.
Best options: Kinetic sand + tools, sensory bin with themed accessories to find
The Therapeutic Action
Begin using tools in the bin yourself (scoop, pour, find hidden object). Don't require child to join — let your engagement draw them. When child touches bin: embed a task immediately: "Can you find the car in there?"
Safety note: Never leave unsupervised. Not suitable for children who mouth objects without close supervision. Duration: 10 minutes.
🛒 Search Amazon.in: "kinetic sand India"

Safety First: Read This Before Every Session
🔴 ABSOLUTE STOP — Do Not Proceed If:
  • Child is showing signs of illness (fever, ear pain, unusual fatigue)
  • Child is already in distress or meltdown state before session
  • Session environment has been recently disrupted (move, family crisis, schedule change)
  • Child has had a medical procedure in the past 48 hours
  • Sensory bins: Child who mouths objects — choking hazard. Skip until mouthing reduces.
  • Magnetic construction sets: Never use with children who mouth objects. Magnet ingestion requires emergency medical attention.
🟡 MODIFY — Proceed With Changes If:
  • Child is tired — shorten session to 5 minutes, reduce demands
  • Child seems dysregulated — start with preferred sensory material first, let them regulate, then gently introduce the play expansion
  • Child is in a "lining phase" — don't interrupt. Sit alongside, model the expansion, don't demand it
🟢 PROCEED — Green Light When:
  • Child is alert, fed, and recently rested
  • Environment is calm and prepared (see next card)
  • Materials are ready and accessible
  • You have 15–20 uninterrupted minutes
  • You are emotionally regulated — your co-regulation is part of the therapy

📞 Unsure about your child's readiness? Call FREE 9100 181 181
Set Up Your Space: Spatial Precision Prevents 80% of Session Failures
Setup Checklist
  • Play mat or carpet defined area — creates "play space" boundary
  • ALL other toys removed from view (reduce competition/distraction)
  • Maximum 2 materials visible at start — introduce others during session
  • Screen off, audio quiet (or gentle instrumental music at low volume)
  • Lighting: warm and moderate — avoid harsh fluorescent overhead
  • Temperature comfortable — child cannot self-regulate if physically uncomfortable
  • Parent positioned BESIDE child (parallel), not across (confrontational)
  • Reinforcement items ready nearby (stickers, preferred snack, praise script memorized)
  • Visual timer visible if child responds to them
Why Parallel Positioning Matters
Face-to-face positioning increases social demand and can trigger avoidance. Side-by-side parallel play respects the child's need for low social pressure while maintaining connection.
This is the OT and ABA consensus position for play expansion sessions. One change in body orientation can transform a session from resistant to engaged.
Materials Placement
Place the materials tray on a low surface accessible to the child's right — within reach but not forced into their hands. The child should be able to choose to engage.

The best session is one that starts right. Before beginning any session, run this quick assessment. Starting when the child is not ready wastes opportunity and can create negative associations with the materials.

Step 1: The Invitation
Every Session Begins With an Invitation. Never a Command.
The Invitation Script
"Hey, come look what I found..."
Place one material within child's visual field — don't hand it. Let them reach.
If child is already playing repetitively:
"I see you're doing that. Can I try too?"
Sit beside, mirror their action briefly, then model the expansion.
Timing: 30–60 seconds max. If no engagement: pause, give space, try again.
Reading the Response
Acceptance looks like: Child looks toward the material even briefly · child moves body toward you · child picks up or touches the material · any vocalization or gesture toward the material
Resistance — how to modify:
Child moves away → reduce distance, try again in 5 min
Child ignores → make the material interesting to you (show delight, don't demand)
Child pushes it away → honor it, try a different material
One second of genuine curiosity is progress. We are building a relationship with functional play. That takes time.
Step 2: The Engagement
Show Don't Tell. Model Don't Demand.
Once child has shown interest or proximity, begin modeling the material's function — with genuine enthusiasm, but without requiring the child to participate. Your delight is the invitation.
Engagement Scripts
"Look at this! When I push this button... WHOA! Something happened!" (Press cause-effect toy — show genuine surprise)
"Watch this car go down the ramp... ready... ready... ZOOM!" (Release car, let the excitement be organic)
How to Present the Material
Speed: Slow reveal, then the exciting action
Distance: Within child's reach but not forced into their hands
Angle: At child's eye level or lower — never looming
Duration: 60–90 seconds of modeling before any gentle offering
Child Response Indicators
🟢 Engagement: Moves toward, reaches, vocalizes, imitates action
🟡 Tolerance: Watches, doesn't leave, continues nearby
🔴 Avoidance: Moves away, pushes back, escalates distress
The moment child makes any move toward the material: "Yes! You see it!" — immediate, warm, specific. Do not wait for full functional use to reinforce.
Step 3: The Therapeutic Action
The Active Ingredient — By Material
This is the core of the session. Once engagement is established, the therapeutic action is the specific interaction with each material that drives functional play development. Duration for this phase: 3–10 minutes depending on material.
Materials 1–3 (Cause-Effect, Ramp, Pretend Set)
Press/release/stir — model the ONE functional action. Celebrate the child's first attempt immediately. Redirect gently and warmly if child uses the toy non-functionally.
Materials 4–5 (Sensory-Match, Action Figures)
Match the toy to the specific sensory preference (spinner → gear; liner → track). Walk figures, narrate minimally. Child's spontaneous interaction counts as functional play.
Material 6 (Bubbles)
Blow bubbles, then pause. Wait for communicative attempt before making more. The pause teaches requesting — one of the most powerful language targets in this protocol.
Materials 7–9 (Construction, Puppets, Sensory Bin)
Build toward a goal, then play with the result. Let puppet approach on its own terms. Begin sensory bin tasks yourself — let engagement draw child in naturally.

Core therapeutic action should occupy 40–60% of total session time (World J Clin Cases Meta-Analysis, 2024)

Universal Satiation Signals
  • Child pushes material away or moves to distant part of room
  • Child escalates their preferred repetitive behavior
  • Child becomes passive, frozen, or begins to show distress cues
The Variation Principle
Introduce ONE variation per session only. Too much novelty defeats the purpose — predictability is therapeutic at this stage. Stability builds trust; trust enables expansion.
Step 5: Reinforce & Celebrate
Celebrate the Attempt. Not Just the Success.
ABA Reinforcement Timing: Within 3 seconds of the target behavior. Every time. Without exception.
What to Celebrate
  • Child LOOKS at the functional toy (visual attention counts)
  • Child TOUCHES material conventionally for 1 second
  • Child PERFORMS one functional action — even imperfect
  • Child WATCHES you model without leaving the area
  • Child SPONTANEOUSLY returns to material without prompt
Praise Scripts — With Language
"YES! You did it! You drove the car! That was amazing driving!"
"Look at those bubbles you made! You blew them all by yourself!"
"You built it! You BUILT it! Let's see it go!"
Praise — Limited Language
Big smile + enthusiastic clapping + immediate preferred reinforcer: sticker, preferred snack, bounce on lap, preferred sensory input. The reinforcer must feel as powerful as the reward of spinning.
Step 6: The Cool-Down
No Session Ends Abruptly. Ever.
How a session ends determines how the next one begins. A well-managed cool-down builds the association: therapy ends, good things follow.
If Child Resists Ending
Do NOT extend the session — this reinforces resistance. Follow through with end calmly and warmly. Offer the preferred activity immediately after. Note in data tracker if ending was challenging.
Post-Session Activity
Immediate preferred activity — the one they love most. This teaches: therapy ends, good things follow. Over time this association makes sessions easier to begin AND end.
Visual timers classified as evidence-based practice for autism (NCAEP, 2020)
Step 7: Capture the Data — Right Now
Data You Capture Now Drives Progress You See Later.
The 60-second post-session tracker takes less time than making a cup of tea — and it creates the longitudinal record that drives personalized protocol adaptation over weeks and months.
Session Date & Material Used
Record the date and which of the 9 materials you used. Over time, patterns emerge about which materials produce the most consistent engagement.
Duration of Functional Engagement
In seconds or minutes. Even "3 seconds" is data. Tracking duration reveals growth that isn't visible day-to-day but is unmistakable week-to-week.
Child's Best Moment
3 words only — e.g., "drove car twice" or "blew bubble independently." This becomes the record of milestones over your child's journey.
Your Confidence Today (1–5)
Your confidence is a therapeutic variable. When it dips, the system flags support. When it rises, the protocol advances. You are part of the data.

Troubleshooting: When It's Not Working
Every challenge has a clinical explanation — and a clinical solution. None of these problems mean the approach is wrong or your child cannot progress. They mean the protocol needs adjustment.
"Child ignores all 9 materials completely"
Solution: Start with Material 4 (Sensory-Match) — find the ONE sensory channel they love most. The sensory profile assessment may be missing. Call 📞 9100 181 181 for OT sensory profile guidance.
"Engages for 2 seconds then returns to wheel-spinning"
Solution: 2 seconds IS progress. Celebrate it. Track duration each session. If average engagement time is increasing even 1 second per week — the protocol is working. Timeline: 8–12 weeks.
"Meltdown when I try to redirect from spinning"
Solution: You are NOT trying to stop the spinning — you're adding options alongside it. Let child spin, sit beside them, model functional play with a different toy simultaneously.
"Can't get through 5 minutes without refusal"
Solution: Session may be too long. Try: 3 minutes only, one material only, child's highest-energy time of day, single undemanding invitation with zero pressure. Build from there.
"Materials keep getting used 'wrong'"
Solution: Expected. Every calm redirect builds a new neural association. The ramp must become more rewarding than the wheel-spin through repetition. This is gradual shaping, not instant switching.
Adapt: Personalize the Protocol for Your Child
Your child is unique. The protocol flexes to meet them — easier or harder, calmer or more animated, shorter or longer. Here is how to calibrate.
Sensory Seeker
Best entry material: Sensory bin (kinetic sand), cause-effect with vibration
Ramp use: Loud crash at bottom = extra reward
Reinforcement: Deep pressure, movement, jumping
Session length: Can extend 20–25 min if engaged
Modeling style: More animated, larger movements
Sensory Avoider
Best entry material: Bubbles (visual, low-touch), simple pretend (familiar objects)
Ramp use: Quiet glide; avoid loud crashes
Reinforcement: Preferred object, sticker, calm verbal praise
Session length: Keep to 10 min max
Modeling style: Quiet, gentle, low-key
Ages 18m–2y
Cause-effect, bubbles, ramp only. No pretend yet.
Ages 2–3y
Add simple pretend (1 function only). Sensory bins.
Ages 3–5y
Add puppets, action figures. Begin building play scripts.
Ages 5–8y
Construction with purpose. Complex figure play. Peer-parallel scenarios.
Week 1–2: Progress Looks Like Tolerance
ACT IV: The Progress Arc
Weeks 1–2 test your faith in the process. Results are not visible yet — but neural pathway formation IS happening. Every exposure, every gentle redirect, every moment of modeled functional play is depositing in the developmental account.
✅ What Progress Looks Like
  • Child tolerates the material being in the room without distress
  • Child glances at material once or twice during session
  • Child allows adult to model near them without moving away
  • Child engages functionally for even 3–5 seconds total
  • Child shows any interest reaction: leaning, reaching, vocalizing
❌ Not Expected Yet (And That's Fine)
  • Consistent functional play
  • Sustained engagement beyond seconds
  • Any pretend play
  • Transfer to new toys
  • Reduced repetitive play at other times

Week 3–4: Neural Pathways Forming
Consolidation Phase — 40% Progress
In weeks 3 and 4, the invisible becomes visible. Patterns emerge. Your child begins to show that they remember — and that memory is the beginning of everything.
Anticipation Appears
Child moves toward the ramp or cause-effect toy before you even set it up. Memory is forming.
Requesting Emerges
Child communicates for the material in any way — gesture, vocalization, leading you by hand. This is language development happening through play.
Duration Increases
Functional engagement extends: 5 seconds → 15 seconds → 30 seconds. Track it — the graph tells the story your daily experience might miss.
Initiation Begins
Child begins the functional action without watching you model first. They have internalized the play schema.
"You may notice YOU are more confident too. By Week 4, you know your child's signals, you know which materials work, and the session rhythm feels more natural. This is you becoming a therapeutic parent — and that skill is permanent."
Weeks 5–8: The Expansion Phase
Expansion Phase — 65% Progress
Weeks 5–8 are when families begin to feel the shift. Functional play is no longer an event — it's becoming a habit. Generalization begins. First symbolic signs emerge.
Generalization
Child uses functional play with similar new toys — a new car gets driven, not spun. The schema has transferred beyond the original training materials.
Extended Duration
Play duration extends to 2–5 minutes of functional engagement. Sustained play is the hallmark of true skill acquisition.
Parallel Play Begins
Child plays near adult or sibling using materials — the first social play milestone. This signals readiness for G-627.
First Symbolic Signs
Child makes sound effects while driving car, stirs pot while saying "mmm" — the first pretend play sparks. The bridge to symbolic play has been crossed.

Progression signal for next technique: When your child demonstrates 3+ minutes of functional play across 3+ different materials, it's time to formally introduce G-627 (Parallel Play Development).
Every Second of Real Play. Celebrate It.
First Ramp Release
First time child releases a car down the ramp intentionally — not flipped for wheels
First Pretend Stir
First time child stirs the pretend pot — even once, even briefly
First Bubbles
First time child blows bubbles themselves with the wand
First Sound Effect
First time child makes a sound during functional play — "zoom," "crash," "mmm"
"My daughter was three and had never played with toys the way other kids did. Dolls lay untouched. Cars were for lining up. The therapist started with cause-effect toys — she was fascinated that pushing buttons made things happen. Then they introduced ramps for her cars — suddenly driving was more exciting than wheel-spinning. Now, at five, she plays with dolls, drives cars on roads she draws, and even creates simple pretend scenarios. She still lines things up sometimes. But she also plays. Real play."
— Parent, Pinnacle Network (Illustrative case; outcomes vary by child profile)
Red Flags: When to Escalate to Your Team
Most challenges resolve with protocol adjustments. The following signs, however, indicate that clinical reassessment is needed. Do not increase protocol intensity independently if any of these are present.
🔴 Contact Your Team If:
  • No engagement with ANY of the 9 materials after 4 weeks of consistent daily protocol
  • Distress significantly increases when materials are introduced (escalating, not settling)
  • Repetitive play becomes more rigid — new patterns emerging, existing ones more extreme
  • Regression in previously acquired play skills
  • No joint attention — child never looks to share the experience of the toy with you
  • Unusual toy use paired with significant language regression or social withdrawal
  • Child shows self-injurious behavior during sessions or transitions
